tier_reason: docs/benchmarks/access.md compares YaFF directly against Protobuf, FlatBuffers and a raw C++ struct (e.g. Flat/100: 25.99 vs 1383.74 vs 54.81 ns), and it states x25-50 and x2-2.5 (flat) and x25 and x3.5 (hot hierarchical) itself. The code is public in benchmarks/access/flat.cpp and hierarchical.cpp (google/benchmark), and docs/benchmarks/overview.md names Clang 20.1.8, a Release build (no extra flags in the benchmark CMakeLists) and an AMD EPYC 7713, so it meets A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang 20.1.8, CMake Release build (CMake's Release default is -O3 -DNDEBUG; no -march or other extra flags in the benchmark CMakeLists), C++20; google/benchmark 1.9.5, FlatBuffers 24.12.23, Protobuf >=5.26 via Conan (the exact Protobuf version is not stated)
corrections.caveats: Very young project (repo created 2026-04-07), first-party benchmark on a single machine (EPYC 7713, DDR4); the authors say only the ratios generalize. The Protobuf timings include ParseFromString/ParseFromArray of the whole message on every iteration, because Protobuf cannot read fields without parsing. So this compares zero-copy field access with parse-plus-access, not serialization speed. The win shrinks sharply with cold random access (~512 MB working set): 206.64 vs 387.48 ns vs Protobuf (~1.9x) and vs 300.13 ns for FlatBuffers (~1.45x). With hot hierarchical access and hand-cached access chains, FlatBuffers is only ~2.1x slower (20.89 vs 9.81 ns), not 3.5x (derived from page data). The Protobuf version is not pinned (Conan protobuf/[>=5.26]). GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the standard Apache-2.0 notice (Copyright 2026 YANDEX LLC).

notes: All numbers in claimed_speedup match the access.md table and the ratios stated in its text. I read both benchmark sources to confirm the methodology: Protobuf is parsed inside the timed loop, while YaFF and FlatBuffers read the buffer in place. The metadata is correct: 531 stars, last commit 2026-09-23, not archived and not a fork.

tier_reason: chronoxor/CppSerialization's README table and per-protocol CppBenchmark reports show SBE at 35/52 ns and Protobuf at 322/351 ns, and the benchmark code is public (performance/sbe_*.cpp, protobuf_*.cpp). The compiler and flags are not stated (only 'Process configuration: release'), so it is not A. It is also a small suite (167 stars) run by the author of a competing format (FastBinaryEncoding), not a well-known independent suite, so it is not B. This matches how the wave-1 verifier tiered Cap'n Proto and zpp::bits from the same suite.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ~9.2x faster serialize (35 ns vs 322 ns) and ~6.75x faster deserialize (52 ns vs 351 ns) than Protobuf (ratios derived from page data)
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 Pro (10 cores, reported 2.4 GHz), 32 GiB RAM, macOS (Darwin 24.5.0). All 15 CppBenchmark reports in the README come from this one machine, run on 2025-07-16
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated; the CppBenchmark reports say only 'Process configuration: release'. The SBE C++ codecs were generated with sbe-all-1.40.1.jar, and Protobuf is built from the protobuf main branch via gil (version not pinned)
corrections.workload: Serialize/deserialize a small trading domain object (one Account with Wallet and 3 Orders, 128 bytes in memory) in chronoxor's CppBenchmark-based CppSerialization suite. SBE encodes it to 138 bytes and Protobuf to 120 bytes. Both timings include converting from/to the plain C++ domain model: Protobuf builds a fresh message per operation without an arena, while SBE encodes in place into a fixed 1 KB buffer. Also compared: Cap'n Proto, FastBinaryEncoding, FlatBuffers, zpp::bits and JSON (RapidJSON).
corrections.caveats: The numbers come from a small third-party shootout (chronoxor/CppSerialization, 167 stars) run by the author of a competing format (FastBinaryEncoding), not by SBE's team. SBE's own sbe-benchmarks (Car/MarketData, C++ and Java) do not compare against Protobuf. Compiler and flags are not stated, and everything ran on a single Apple M1 Pro on 2025-07-16 with SBE 1.40.1. The message is tiny (138 bytes), so the results may not generalize to larger or variable-length-heavy messages. zpp::bits was marginally faster in the same table (34/37 ns).

notes: The numbers match the SBE and Protobuf rows and their detailed reports exactly. I downgraded B to C because the suite is neither well-known nor fully neutral, and compiler and flags are missing. The record's claim that the repo logs 'several per-run hardware configs' is wrong: every report is the same M1 Pro. The metadata is correct (Apache-2.0, 3,511 stars, last commit 2026-09-17, active).

tier_reason: The first-party benchmarks/cpp/README.md table compares Fory against Protobuf (e.g. MediaContent serialize 2,254,915 vs 504,410 ops/s, 4.5x). The code is public (benchmarks/cpp/benchmark.cc, Google Benchmark) and the flags are stated (-O3 -DNDEBUG, Release), but the compiler is not stated and the CPU model is not named (arm64, 12 cores, 48 GB only), so it is C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build with explicit -O3 -DNDEBUG (benchmarks/cpp/CMakeLists.txt), C++17; Protobuf v25.5, Google Benchmark v1.9.1 and msgpack-c cpp-6.1.0 via FetchContent. The compiler and its version are not stated
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (Apache Fory's own repo); the CPU model and compiler are not disclosed. The README table's numbers have not changed since at least 2026-03-23; commit 7f8e2237ec on 2026-05-08 only renamed a row. A newer generated report (docs/benchmarks/object-serialization/xlang/cpp/README.md, 2026-06-12, Darwin 24.6.0, the same 12-core/48 GB arm64 machine) has Fory 1.27x-10.9x faster than Protobuf, e.g. MediaContent serialize 8,808,084 vs 2,122,926 ops/s (4.15x) and SampleList serialize 3,864,068 vs 353,391 (10.9x) (ratios derived from page data). Fory also beats msgpack-c there. The Protobuf timings for NumericStruct, MediaContent and the list cases include converting to/from a plain C++ struct on every iteration (to_pb_*/from_pb_*), while Sample uses native protobuf objects and shows the smallest gain in the README table (1.3x). Fory runs in xlang compatible mode and reuses its output buffer.
